RELATIVE ATOMIC MASS 22

Because individual atoms are so small, units such as the gram are too large for describing low numbers of
atoms. Atomic mass units (amu) are the basic units of mass for atoms. One amu is equal to 1.66 x 10” kg.

Chemists need a standard against which they can compare atoms. The first standard was hydrogen (the
simplest atom) which gave a hydrogen atom a mass of 1.0000 amu. Later, naturally-occurring oxygen
was used instead of hydrogen and assigned a mass of 16.0000 amu. However, oxygen exists as Isotopes,
where some atoms have a different number of neutrons and hence different masses. In 1961 the isotope
carbon-12 ("C) was adopted as the standard measure and one atom of carbon-12 is defined as having a
mass of 12 amu, In other words, the mass of 1 amu is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom,

Because the masses of all atoms are compared to this standard, they are often called relative atomic
masses (relative meaning compared to each other). Some older textbooks refer to atomic mass units as
daltons, named after John Dalton (1766-1844).

Most Periodic Tables give relative atomic masses as well as atomic numbers, Remember:
* Atomic number is the number of protons (and is also equal to the number of electrons)
* Atomic mass (mass number) is the number of protons plus the number of neutrons

* Relative atomic masses of elements are often not whole numbers because in nature they are
mixtures of isotopes

© The term atomic weight is often used instead of atomic mass.

INTRODUCTION TO CARBON CHEMISTRY 1

Organic chemistry

Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. At one time, the term ‘organic compound’ meant
a compound that was found in plant or animal materials, such as sugars, fats and proteins. All of these
compounds contain carbon. Now the term organic compounds is used for almost all carbon compounds,
whether they come from plants and animals or are made in a laboratory. However, compounds such as
carbonates (-CO,*) and carbon dioxide are not usually described as organic compounds.

1 What is the formula for carbon dioxide?

About 5 million chemical compounds are known to occur on Earth. Over 4 million of these are carbon
compounds. However, the Earth contains less than 0.01 % by mass of carbon. This huge discrepancy
between the proportion of compounds that contain carbon and the proportion of carbon in the Earth
indicates that carbon atoms have some very unusual bonding properties. The bonding in most organic
substances is covalent.

2 Does covalent bonding involve sharing electrons or the transfer of electrons?

Carbon is in Group [V of the Periodic Table and has four electrons in the outer shell, Because of this, it
tends to form four covalent bonds, The four electrons available in the outer shell also allows for a much
larger number of possible combinations with other atoms. This enables carbon to form

many different molecules and explains why it is present in so many compounds,

SEPARATING GASES FROM THE ATMOSPHERE

‘The gases that surround Earth are known as its atmosphere. The atmosphere is a source of many
important gases. These gases can be obtained from the air by fractional distillation. In this process,

air is compressed and cooled until it is a liquid. The temperature is gradually increased and gases are
distilled off in the order of their boiling points.

The gas with the lowest boiling point will be the first to vaporise and be distilled off. As the temperature
continues to rise, the gas with the next lowest boiling point will vaporise, and so on. The gas with the
highest boiling point will be the last to be distilled. Figure 1 shows a simplified version of how two gases
separate during this process.

CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM 27

Generally changes of state are reversible; for example, liquid water can be changed to solid ice and vice
versa. Most chemical reactions are theoretically reversible. This means that not only do reactants form
products; but (depending on conditions) products can be changed back to the original reactants.
Equilibrium reactions are special types of reversible reactions,

Alexander William Williamson (1824-1904) was the first person to systematically study reversible
reactions, He was also the first person to come up with the concept of dynamic equilibrium, Dynamic
equilibrium describes the equilibrium, or balance, of forward and reverse reactions happening simultane-
ously, Therefore an equilibrium reaction involves two reactions that are occurring at the same time but
in opposite directions, In other words, reactants are being changed to products at the same time that
products are being changed to reactants. At equilibrium, the rates of the forward reactions and reverse
reactions are the same. This is shown by using the equilibrium symbol (=).

For example: Products « Reactants

heated in a closed vessel, at first the only reaction will be calcium carbonate decomposing to form
calcium oxide and carbon dioxide. When the pressure and the concentration of calcium oxide and
carbon dioxide reach a certain point, they start to react to form calcium carbonate. This is shown by the
equation: CaCO, (s) « CaO (s) + CO, (g)

ENERGY AND REACTIONS

'

Potential energy is energy that is stored and ‘waiting’ to be used. Chemical energy, i.e. the energy stored
in chemicals, is a type of potential energy. Chemical energy is used to keep living things alive. The
energy stored in food is broken down by the body to be used as fuel for the body’s metabolic activities.
(Metabolism is the sum of all of the chemical processes occurring in the body.) Chemical energy can be
converted to heat, electricity and light (and vice-versa). The energy released or absorbed by a chemical
reaction can be measured. Chemists tend to focus on measuring changes in heat energy.

1 Food energy is broken down to be used to fuel the body’s metabolic activities. Name three ways the

body uses this energy.

2 How can heat changes in a chemical reaction be measured?

heat) and is given the symbol H. (Enthalpy is actually a little more complex than
this definition). A change in heat energy is written as AH. The symbol A (delta)

means ‘a change’, It is usually not possible to measure the total amount of

enthalpy in a system, but it is possible to measure changes, Some reactions give — is
out heat (are exothermic), other reactions take in heat from their surroundings (are

endothermic).

REACTION PROFILES

Potential energy diagrams are very useful in studying energy changes of reactions. They show:
* energy levels of reactants
* energy levels of products
* activation energy
* enthalpy change for the reaction.

Energy must be added to start a reaction. This is because an energy barrier (e.g. to break bonds) must be
overcome. An energy barrier separates substances used in a reaction (reactants) from the products
created. Overcoming the barrier to enable one substance to be converted into another requires the input
of energy. This energy input is called the Activation Energy (E,). Activation energy is the minimum
amount of energy required to allow a reaction to occur; for example, the head of a match will burst into
flame when it is struck ~ the heat from the friction starts the reaction.

1 Name another reaction that requires energy to start it.
For some reactions the energy available at room temperature is enough to overcome the activation
energy. These reactions are said to be spontaneous. Iron rusting is a spontaneous reaction.

Many chemical reactions occur in solutions. There are two parts to a solution: a solute and a solvent.
The solute is the substance being dissolved. The solvent is the substance in which the solute is being
dissolved. Water is a very common solvent. Concentrations of solutions can be measured in two ways:

Mass/mass states how much of a solute is dissolved in a given mass of solution. A solution of magnesium
chloride (MgCl,) can be described as 5 g/100 g. This means that 5 g of the solute (magnesium chloride)
has been dissolved in 100 g of solution.

Mass/volume states how much of a solute is dissolved in a given volume of a solution. To make
comparing solutions easier, the volume used is usually one litre. A solution of magnesium chloride stated
to be 50 g L* has SO grams of solute dissolved in each litre of solution.

DISSOLVING AND DISSOCIATING

A general (but not infallible) rule says like dissolves like. This means that polar solvents tend to dissolve
polar/ionic substances and non-polar solvents tend to dissolve non-polar substances.
Remember, in a solution:

* the solvent and solute particles are evenly distributed (homogenous) throughout the solution

* the solute particles are too small to be seen

* there are forces of attraction between solvent and solute particles.
Before a substance can dissolve in water the forces between its particles and between water molecules
must be broken, This results in new bonds being formed between the water and the solute. Breaking
bonds requires energy to be put in (endothermic; endo: within); making bonds gives energy out
(exothermic; exo: outside). If a covalent molecule is very large (it can consist of tens of thousands of
atoms, e.g. cellulose and polythene) or is non-polar, it will not dissolve in water. The bonding in
covalent network structures (e.g. diamond and silicon dioxide) is too strong to be overcome by any
possible bonds between particles in the structure and water molecules.

to gases. Common standards include 1 atmosphere pressure (sometimes quoted as 101.3 kPa) and either
0°C (273 K) or 25°C (298 K).

THE MOLE

Many everyday names represent a fixed number of objects. For example:

* a soccer team: 11 * adozen eggs: 12

* anetball team: 7 a gross of woodscrews: 144
* a hockey team: 11 a ream of paper; 500 sheets
* an Australian Rules football team: 18 a century of runs: 100

1 Give another name that stands for a fixed quantity.

Chemistry is all about objects like atoms, molecules and ions, These objects are all so small that there
must be many billions of them before they can be seen. A special number used in chemistry is 6.02 x 10",
called the mole. It is also called Avogadro’s number, in honour of Amedeo Avogadro (1776-1856). The
mole is simply a convenient unit of measurement that chemists use because it fits in with ‘natural’
numbers. It is like saying there are 365 days in a year, the diameter of the Earth is 12 800 km, light
travels at 300 000 kilometres per second (approximately), and so on.

Units of measurement are often used in mathematics questions:
EXAMPLES
i How many dozens (units of 12) are there in 36 units?
Divide the total number by the number in one dozen: 36 + 12 = 3 dozen.

ii How many days are there in 100 hours?
00 + 24 = 4.17 days

The same mathematic principles apply to calculations with moles.
EXAMPLES

ili How many atoms of sodium are there in 0.5 moles of sodium?

‘Of is a hint to use multiplication, Multiply the number of moles by the number of atoms in a mole:
0.5 x 6.02 x 10" = 3.01 x 10”

iv How many moles of water molecules are in 57 x 10” particles of water?
Divide the total number of particles by the number of particles that makes up a mole:
57 x 10” + 6.02 x 10" = 9.5 x 10"

(Note that when using moles we sometimes get ‘silly’ or ‘ridiculously large’ numbers.)

DEPENDABILITY OF INFORMATION

In chemistry you need to be able to:

* design and carry out first-hand investigations

* discuss first-hand investigations

* collect information from secondary sources

* assess information from secondary sources

* decide on the reliability of the results you obtain from your work

First-hand investigations are those that you carry out yourself, e.g. practicals in the laboratory. Secondary
sources include textbooks and encyclopaedias.

from other secondary sources of information?

Variables

During experiments, we often concentrate on observing and recording what happens when conditions
change. Factors that can be changed during an experiment are called variables. Usually only one
variable is changed at a time during an experiment. There are four major groups of variables.

* independent

* dependent

* controlled

* uncontrolled.

‘The independent variable is the major part of the hypothesis (belief) that you are testing. It is the
condition that you change to see what happens. The dependent variable is the feature that changes as a
direct result of changing the independent variable. A controlled variable is one that is kept the same in
each experiment. An uncontrolled variable is one that has not been taken into account during the
planning of the experiment.

EXTRACTION AND REFINING OF METALS

In order to extract metals from their ores, energy is needed. The more reactive the metal, the more
difficult it is to decompose (break down) its ore.

Copper The most important ores, the sulfides, contain between 1 and 12 percent of copper. Ores are
mined and then crushed and concentrated by flotation. This technique allows comparatively heavy
substances to float on water. Finely-ground copper ore is mixed with water and flotation reagents are
added, Air is blown through this mixture to form a froth. The froth mixes with the sulfide but not with
the other substances. The ore floats to the top, leaving other substances behind. Oxides and carbonates
of copper are reduced (oxygen, etc. removed) with carbon. Sulfides are smelted in a furnace, resulting in
copper that is approximately 98 percent pure, This can be further purified to 99.9 percent through
electrolysis. Electrolysis uses large amounts of electricity to attract pure copper to an electrode,

1 Define each term,

a energy b sulfide ¢ flotation d reagent e reactive
2 Draw a flow chart to show the production of copper metal from its ore.

Iron is extracted from iron ore (haematite) in a blast furnace, Coke (a form of carbon) and limestone
(calcium carbonate) are added with iron ore to a blast furnace where the raw materials are strongly
heated. The coke provides the heat to produce carbon monoxide (CO) which takes the oxygen from the
iron oxide. The limestone removes impurities, which melt in the furnace and are removed as slag. Hot
air is blown in near the bottom of the furnace. The molten iron produced is then cast into ingots. This
cast iron usually requires further treatment before it can be used.

3 Suggest why it is important to remove impurities from substances being mined.
4 Draw a flow chart to show the production of iron metal from its ore.

METALS 13

Metals are found on the left-hand side and centre of the Periodic Table. Most metals are lustrous (shiny)
and they are often silver in colour. Metals are good thermal and electrical conductors, whereas most
non-metals are poor conductors.

1 What is meant by @ good thermal conductor?

Metals are malleable; they can be beaten into shape. They are also ductile; they can be drawn into wires.
Non-metals are brittle; they snap instead of bend. Metals are usually denser than non-metals. Metals are
solids at room temperature (with the exception of mercury, Hg). They usually have high melting points.
Very few metals occur native (uncombined) in the natural state. They are usually found combined with
other elements. The earliest metals to be used by humans were copper (Cu), tin (Sn), silver (Ag) and gold
(Au) - all of these metals can be found native.

2 Explain why copper, tin, silver and gold can be found native.
Very few metals occur uncombined in the natural state. They are usually found chemically joined with
other elements in minerals. A mineral is a naturally-occurring pure substance. An ore is a material from
the Earth’s crust that contains enough of a substance to make it worth mining. Iron (Fe) exists in the
forms of haematite and magnetite, which are both forms of iron oxide (i.e, iron combined with oxygen
in a compound). Iron ore is very similar in chemical composition to iron rust.
Aluminium (Al) is found as bauxite (aluminium oxide) and lead (Pb) as galena (lead sulfide, lead
combined with sulfur). Copper occurs in the ores malachite and azurite, which are both forms of copper
carbonate. Another important ore of copper is chalcopyrite, a yellow mineral consisting of sulfides of
copper and iron.

Reactivity of metals

water, acids and alkalis. Metals such as gold (Au) and silver (Ag) are very unreactive.

Recycling metals

Our supply of metals or minerals is limited by how much of them is in the ground and how much of
that is obtainable. Since 1950, more metals have been used up than in the whole history of the world
before 1950. It is difficult to estimate how long our supply of metals will last, so we should be more
careful about how much metal we waste. As metals become more expensive, recycling becomes more
attractive. Producing copper from scrap costs about 4% of the cost of making it from its ore. Today about
50% of copper and about 80% of the lead from car batteries is recycled. About 20% of aluminium and
18% of iron (as steel) is recycled.

HARD WATER 18]

When soap solution is added to soft water and shaken, a lather (foam) readily forms. If soap solution is
added to hard water, lather does not form immediately, More soap has to be added until it removes all of
the hardness. Hardness in water wastes soap. Other indications of hard water include hard deposits in
hot water systems and kettles. Synthetic (‘soapless') detergents are not affected by hard water.
There are two sorts of hardness: temporary and permanent. Temporary hardness is caused by carbonates
and can be removed by boiling. Permanent hardness is not removed by boiling. Chemicals called water
softeners can be used to remove hardness so that less soap is needed. Dissolved calcium (Ca) and
magnesium (Mg™) tons are a major source of hardness, Water can also be ‘softened’ by passing it through
an ion exchange medium, where calcium and magnesium ions are replaced by sodium ions. The
medium is usually made up of organic resins and can be regenerated by passing brine (salt solution)
through it. Chemical water softeners work in a different way; they react with these ions and remove
them from solution by precipitating them out.

Water is treated before it is supplied to the mains, Each water authority has its own treatment procedure
dependent upon the initial quality of water, but the following procedure is fairly typical.

Water from a dam passes through large mesh filters to trap any large objects. The water is clarified (made

a bed of sand. The water is then aerated by cascading through waterfalls or in artificial fountains. This
removes odours and tastes by oxidising them. The water can be softened (calcium and magnesium ions
removed) by the addition of lime (CaO) and soda (Na,CO,). At this stage there may still be microorganisms

The quality of water is determined by many factors. Two important considerations are the amount of
oxygen dissolved in the water sample and the biological oxygen demand (BOD) of that sample. BOD is
an indication of how much oxygen is needed by organisms in a sample of water.

Oxygen becomes dissolved in water in many ways; including by diffusing from the atmosphere, by
aeration (rapid movement) and by underwater green plants.

In 1661, Robert Boyle (1627-1691) published a work called The Sceptical Chymist in which, among other
things, he distinguished between acids and bases (although he referred to bases as alkalis). He noted that
all acids turned a particular vegetable indicator from blue to red and all alkalis turned the indicator
green. Boyle found that some substances did not change the colour of this indicator and he concluded
that these substances were neutral. Around this time it was also proposed that salts are formed when
acids react with bases.

Antoine Laurent Lavoisier (1743-1794) was one of the first people to investigate what was responsible for
giving an acid its properties. By 1776 he had come to the conclusion that one element was present in all
of the acids he knew; hence this element must cause an acid to behave as it does. This element was
oxygen, named from the Greek terms oxein (sour) and gennen (to generate). Lavoisier was wrong, because
he only knew the formulae of a few acids.

the substance being dissolved.) When dealing with solutions of acids and bases, chemists usually use

percentage of molecules ionised in solution than a weak acid does.

ROLES OF CHEMISTS

You may need a textbook and/or dictionary to help you with this worksheet.

There are many roles that chemists play in modern society. Four main areas are:
* industry * pure research * education * community work
1 Read the following passages and define each term in italics.

Chemists Three branches of chemistry are organic, inorganic and physical. Organic chemistry
involves the study of carbon compounds; inorganic chemistry is the study of compounds not
based on carbon; and physical chemistry is concerned with the physical characteristics of matter.

Industry In our world we depend on manufactured goods and there are many different
industries that produce these goods. For example, chemists can be found working in the
metal, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, agriculture, fibre, cosmetics, food and electronic
industries. Industrial chemists tend to be employed in quality controf and research and
development, Chemists working in quality control ensure that the standard of goods produced
is of the required quality. This means checking raw materials as they come into a factory and
carrying out an analysis to make certain these materials are what they are supposed to be.
Chemists need to check at many stages of the manufacturing process that conditions such as
temperature, concentration of solutions and pressure are within specified margins. Chemists
are also responsible for ensuring that factory emissions do not exceed specified limits. Research
and development (R & D) is a process that improves existing products and manufacturing
processes, and designs new ones. The properties of materials are investigated and these
materials can be altered or used in new ways. The use of computers has speeded up much of
the research done by chemists and many processes have been automated.

SULFUR

Sulfur (sometimes spelt sulphur) is a yellow, brittle solid at room temperature. It doesn’t dissolve in water
but is soluble in some organic (carbon-based) solvents such as methylbenzene. Being a typical non-metal,
sulfur does not conduct electricity and has a low melting point (approx 115°C). Sulfur was called
brimstone in old books, It occurs as the almost pure element in underground deposits (¢.g. those found
in Sicily and the USA). It is the sixteenth most-abundant element in the Earth’s crust.

Sulfur is in Group VI in the Periodic Table and so sulfur atoms have six
electrons in the outer (valence) shell. Figure 1 shows how the electrons are
arranged in an atom of sulfur. Sulfur forms many compounds; e.g. oxides,
sulfides, sulfites and sulfates. Sulfur dioxide (SO,), iron (II) sulfide (FeS),
sodium sulfite (Na,SO,) and copper sulfate (CuSO,) are common examples of
sulfur compounds.

The most important use of sulfur is in the manufacture of sulfur compounds
such as sulfuric acid (H,SO,) which is a very important industrial chemical.
It is important in medicine for ‘sulfa’ (sulphonamide) drugs and in many
skin treatments, Sulfur is also a raw material in the manufacture of matches,
rubber tyres, dyes and gunpowder.

When sulfur burns in air, it gives a blue flame, forming sulfur dioxide. This is a colourless, heavier-than-
air gas. Sulfur dioxide Is also formed when fossil fuels such as coal and oil are burned, Coal usually
contains 0.5%-5% sulfur. Sulfur dioxide has a very irritating smell and is poisonous even at low levels. It
is thought to contribute to bronchitis and other lung diseases, Sulfur dioxide is acidic and has bleaching
properties. This compound can be used to kill germs and, at low concentrations, as a food preservative,
as it prevents the growth of moulds and bacteria.

THE ATMOSPHERE 2

The Noble gases In 1904 Sir William Ramsay was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discover-
ing a new Group of elements, the Noble gases. This Group is now known to consist of helium (He), neon
(Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe) and radon (Rn). Radon was discovered by Fredrich Ernst Dorn
in 1898. These gases are all colourless, tasteless and very unreactive. They are unreactive because they
have full outer (valence) electron shells. In total, the Noble gases make up around 1% of the earth’s
atmosphere (by volume); argon is by far the most common. Although helium is estimated to make up
around 23% of the material in the Universe, it only makes up about 0.0005% of Earth’s atmosphere.
Helium (from the Greek word Helios, meaning Sun) is used in cryogenics because it can (when liquid)
reach temperatures very close to absolute zero (-273.15°C). Cryogenics is the science that deals with the
behaviour of materials at very low temperatures (cryo: icy; genic; produced by nature). Another use of
helium is in lighter-than-air balloons.

When neon (from the Greek neos, meaning new) gas has an electric current argon gas
passed through it while under low pressure, the gas emits a reddish light.
This makes neon useful in making advertising signs and also in some lasers. eee

reactive metals to provide an inert atmosphere to stop the metals from
reacting with oxygen. Light globes can also contain argon. In these globes a
thin tungsten (W) wire glows white-hot when an electric current is passed
through it. The inside of the globe is filled with argon.

and glass. The Solvay (ammonia-soda) process was invented by Ernest Solvay (1838-1922) in the mid
18605. It is a multistage process that involves the recycling of most of the by-products involved in the
manufacture of the sodium carbonate.

replenish that lost during the process. It is a cyclical procedure, but the following sequence will help in

carbon dioxide (CO,).

C The temperature is kept below 15°C to ensure that the sodium hydrogencarbonate (slightly-soluble)

D The sodium hydrogencarbonate is heated to form sodium carbonate, carbon dioxide and water.

Nuclear chemistry studies the nucleus (centre) of atoms, In 1909, Ernest Rutherford was the first person
to come up with the idea that the nucleus of an atom was very small, dense and positively charged.
Rutherford calculated that the radius of an atom would be in the order of 10" m and the radius of the
nucleus would be approximately 10" m.

1 How does the size of the radius of the nucleus compare to that of the whole atom?

Shortly after this (1913) it was calculated that the protons of an individual atom made up about half of
the mass of the nucleus. Hence there must be some other (unknown) particles making up the ‘missing’
mass. The concept of atomic number (Z) came into use around this time. The atomic number of a
particular atom of an element shows:

* the number of electrons

¢ the number of protons

© the order in which the element is listed in the Periodic Table.
In 1932, James Chadwick discovered that inside atoms there were uncharged particles with a mass
approximately that of a proton. We now call this particle a neutron and know that it is located inside
the nucleus.

All atoms of an element have the same atomic number (Z), but some atoms have a different atomic mass
(A). This is because they can have different numbers of neutrons in the nucleus. Atoms of the same
elements that have different masses are called isotopes. English physicist Francis Aston (1877-1945) was
awarded a Nobel Prize in 1922 for his invention of the mass spectrograph. This machine can show the
relative percentages present of different isotopes of the same element.

Proteins are needed in the body for the growth and repair of tissues and to help certain chemical
reactions take place. They are used as an energy source only under extreme conditions. (Energy is the
capacity to do work.)

PROBLEMS WITH PLASTICS?

y

Plastics have been described as being ‘too good’. They have become popular because they:

© are made from relatively cheap raw materials * are good thermal and electrical insulators
(petrochemicals) * have good safety and hygiene properties for

* can be moulded and shaped or drawn into fibres packaging food and medicines

* are tough * are lighter than alternatives

* can be coloured * are resistant to chemicals,

The world’s annual consumption of plastic materials has increased from around 5 million tonnes in the
1950s to nearly 100 million tonnes today. Plastics degrade very slowly. No one knows how long they
take to break down because plastics have only been in existence for a relatively short time. Degrading
slowly is a useful property while plastics are being used, but a problem when plastics are discarded. The
disposal of plastics causes problems; e.g. they can give off toxic fumes when burnt. Many people think
that less plastic should be used. Other people claim that plastics are an essential part of modern living;
e.g. the use of plastics has made cars lighter and more fuel-efficient. There are ways that the amount of
plastic thrown away can be reduced.

* Use less plastic; e.g. use alternative (conventional) products

© Recycle

* Develop biodegradable plastics.

are given out and discarded in Australia every year. Many retail businesses are trying to discourage cust-
omers from using plastic bags by charging for them and by suggesting alternative ways of carrying goods.

When a metal is attacked by air, water or other substances, the metal is said to corrode. Usually the
more reactive a metal is, the more readily it corrodes, The most common example of corrosion is the
rusting of iron. Corrosion is an oxidation process, Remember, oxidation involves any (or all) of the
following:

© addition of oxygen
* loss of electrons
* loss of hydrogen.

commonly used structural material; it is strong, easily shaped and reasonably cheap. However, it rusts in
damp air.

When iron corrodes, rust forms in flakes, Damp air can get past the flakes and attack the metal below.
Given enough time, a piece of iron can rust all the way through.

grease to keep out air and water. Galvanising is a process that covers iron (or steel) with a coating of

scratched. Rust is hydrated iron oxide and has the formula Fe,O,.xH,O, where x can be a number

Redox is an abbreviation for the terms reduction and oxidation, Like many expressions in chemistry,
their meanings of reduction and oxidation have evolved. Because oxygen is involved in so many
common reactions (such as burning, corrosion, respiration and photosynthesis) many chemists have
studied it. Oxidation originally meant the addition of oxygen to an element; reduction originally meant
the removal of oxygen. Gradually, electronic theory and the concept of valency expanded, and oxidation
and reduction have been related to the transfer or rearrangement of electrons. This in turn has led to the
ideas of reduction and oxidation being applied to most reactions.

1 The property of elements that determines the ratio of combining atoms of different elements. What does
this describe?

Here are some broader definitions of oxidation:
* The complete or partial removal of electrons from an atom
* The loss of electrons.

Here are some broader definitions of reduction:

* The complete or partial addition of electrons to an atom

© The gain of electrons.
There seems to be a contradiction here, Electrons are particles with a single charge — how can they be
partially removed? The answer lies in the following descriptions;

* Ionic bonding involves one atom transferring one or more electrons to a different atom

* Covalent bonding has atoms sharing electrons

* Polar covalent bonding has unequal sharing of electrons.
Polar covalent bonding shows characteristics of both ionic and covalent bonding. Electrons are shared,
but one atom has a greater share of the electron pair.

a tonic b Covalent ¢ Polar covalent

K\ Cell Division I

Cell division plays an essential role in the growth, repair and reproduction of

multicellular organisms. Cell division is the splitting of one (parent) cell = >
into two identical (daughter) cells. There are two main types of cell
division — mitosis and meiosis. Cells fall into two main classes somatic
cells and germ cells.

When human sex cells (gametes) join at fertilisation they produce a single cell (a zygote). This cell starts
to divide and, after nine months (and billions of cell divisions), a baby is born,

There are thin, thread-like, microscopic structures called chromosomes present in the nucleus of a cell.
The chromosomes can only be seen when a cell is dividing. Chromosomes occur in cells in pairs (apart
from in sex cells), Humans have 23 pairs (2n) of chromosomes. Other species have different numbers
of chromosomes. Chromosomes are strands of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid), and consist of sections
called genes. These contain the instructions for controlling cells, and need to be able to be copied
precisely, because a mistake made early in replication will be repeated in every cell.

There are two processes by which cells can divide: mitosis and meiosis. In mitosis the cell continues to
duplicate and divide, producing daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell. These are

needed for growth and to replace the millions of cells that die every day.

\\, DNA I

DNA: the molecular basis of heredity, found in cell nuclei, consisting of a double helix held
together by weak bonds between bases which project inward from two chains.

Compared to other molecules, DNA is huge and amazing. However, it is made up of only a few
substances: four nitrogen ‘bases’, a sugar and phosphates. The four bases are adenine (A), thymine (T),
cytosine (C) and guanine (G). A base, a sugar and a phosphate form a three-part unit called a nucleotide.
‘The sugar involved is deoxyribose, hence the name deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA,

Base-pairing

In the same way that jigsaw puzzles fit together, nucleotides have specific
pairing rules. Adenine on one strand will pair with thymine on the other, and
guanine on one strand will pair with cytosine, producing a ladder-like structure,
pulled together by hydrogen bonds into a coil shape, known as a double helix.

The diagram on the right shows a short sequence on a DNA ‘ladder’.
1 | Copy the diagram, using the pairing rules to identify the bases labelled ‘7’.
[2 | What do the dotted lines between the bases represent?

Although the amount and proportions of the nitrogen bases vary in all species, the four bases are all
present and always follow the base pairing rules: A with T, and G with C.

Hint: think Ginger Cake. Ginger and Cakes go well together, and so do G and C. If you
remember this, that leaves the pairing of A and T remaining by default.

The genetic code can be compared to a four letter alphabet: A, G, C and T. These bases spell the genetic
‘words’, and these groups of words are known as genes. The language of DNA is a language of proteins.
Proteins are made of polypeptide chains.

Replication

When DNA replicates (produces a copy of itself), it unwinds and unzips first. The bonds that held the
complementary bases together break and each half of the ‘zipper’ is used as a template (model) on
which new DNA will be built.

K\ DNA: the raw material of genetics

Genetics is the study of inheritance — how characteristics are passed from one generation to the next.
Genetic material is stored in the nucleus of each cell. The major bodies involved in this process are
called chromosomes, Each chromosome is made up of genes. Genes are the instructions that are
responsible for the components and appearance of an organism. They are found in the nucleus of a cell.

A gene: ihe part of a chromosome that determines the inheritance of a characteristic or of a group of
characteristics.

Each chromosome is made of a single molecule of DNA. The DNA molecule is a chain of many genes
connected together. DNA is a nucleic acid and is a very large molecule. If the DNA in a single cell was
uncoiled and put in a straight line, it would be a metre long. The backbone of the DNA molecule is two
chains wound around each other, forming a shape rather like a twisted ladder, called a double helix.
There are a large number of smaller molecules (amino acids) attached. The order in which these side
groups are attached determines the code of a particular nucleic acid. The code tells the cell how to
reproduce itself. Cells divide in an organism for growth, repair and reproduction.

Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize for their contributions to the understanding of
the genetic code. Watson and Crick came up with our current double helix (spiral) model of DNA. In
humans each DNA molecule is thought to contain from a few to many thousand genes. Each gene can
be thought of as a series of ‘rungs’ on the DNA ‘ladder’.

J\ Africanis: the world’s last pure breed of dog?

The Africanis, a breed of dog native to Africa for over 70 centuries, is believed to be the last remaining
pure breed of dog, in the truest meaning of the term ‘pure bred’. It possesses features of a breed whose
gene pool has been directed by natural selection alone and not by human intervention. As for all pure-
bred animals, individuals share similarities. In the case of the Africanis these are:

* a related gene pool * medium size
* overall head and body shape ® friendly, intelligent and alert personality
* short fur ® fitness, active behaviour and general good health.

Because natural selection has acted on the Africanis gene pool, it remains richly varied. For this reason,
although the overall appearance of the breed is recognisable, each dog has individual characteristics.
These differences include different:

* colouring
= markings (solid colour or multiple colour markings).

These differences make the breed particularly attractive to humans because a choice of ‘models’ is
available. People can select a look that most appeals to them, In order to safeguard the future of the
Africanis, it has recently been officially recognised as a breed in the hopes it will not be interfered with
or left to interbreed with other types of dog, producing mongrels.

Evolution: a theory describing the processes that have transformed life on Earth from its earliest forms

Evolution and Mutation

Genes are the potential of an organism. The environment may or

may not allow the full development of this potential. Genes are Bole)
contained in chromosomes in the nucleus of cells. Genes are short iS) Py e-Q<

lengths of chromosomes and are the basic unit of inheritance. They © )
usually copy themselves exactly each time a cell divides (meiosis and mitosis) but,

occasionally, the unexpected happens — and the unexpected is usually (but not always) unpleasant.

Genes are made of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), which has a very complicated structure. If this
structure is altered in any way, a different gene may result. This is called mutation. Alleles are different
genes that influence one characteristic. Mutations can remove one allele and replace it with another.

Mutations very rarely occur spontaneously — perhaps one in a million may happen without apparent
cause. The rate is increased by substances called mutagens. Some of these are produced by the cell
themselves and others come from the environment. These include:

* some chemicals
= radiation
= increased temperature.

Chemicals that are suspected of being mutagens include nitrous acid (HNO,) and nitroso compounds
which are present in treated meats such as salami and bacon, mustard gas (used in warfare), tobacco
tars, and fungi that spoil foods. (Some of these substances may also cause cancer — they are
carcinogenic.)

Radiation includes gamma radiation (a form of nuclear radiation), X-rays, cosmic rays (from space) and
ultraviolet (UV) light. There are also natural radioactive sources from the Earth itself. The ozone layer
Protects us from much of the harmful radiation from space, but this has been damaged by such man-
made chemicals as CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons).

An increase in temperature can cause a five-fold increase in the rate of mutations. Violent temperature
changes can cause an even greater change in rate.

If mutations occur in gametes (germ or sex cells), they are inherited.

)A\ Rabbits and Myxomatosis

In 1859, Thomas Austin of Barwon Park Estate, Western Victoria, brought a consignment of rabbits to
Australia from England and released them on his property for hunting purposes. They bred slowly at first
but, after three years, they had become acclimatised and began to reach pest proportions.
About this time a bushfire destroyed part of the fence around Austin’s property. Rabbits
escaped and spread dramatically.

Six years after their introduction, Austin killed 20 000 rabbits on his own property
and estimated that there were at least another 10 000 still at large. By 1879 they were
in New South Wales and, within a short time, they had spread over 75% of the
continent, causing extensive damage to grazing land.

Rabbits had not been a serious pest in England despite their very high birth rate. This was because, in
England, they had various ‘natural enemies’ which preyed on them and kept the population down.
‘These natural enemies did not exist in Australia. Because of rabbit burrows and the habit of eating roots
in dry seasons, the rabbit has destroyed areas which would otherwise have regenerated with the return
of favourable rainfall. In this way, one rabbit can displace many sheep and cattle from a pasture.

Large sums of money were spent on trapping, poisoning, destruction of warrens and gassing but to no
avail. In theory, one pair of rabbits, in ideal conditions, could multiply to 13 million rabbits in three
years. Finally in the early 1950s, it was decided to try biological control. Specimens of the myxoma virus
(originally found in South America) were injected into a few rabbits which were then released. The
myxoma virus is carried by fleas and mosquitoes from live rabbits, and it spread very rapidly. By 1955,
90% of the rabbit population had died of the resulting disease, myxomatosis.

Alfred Wallace was an English naturalist who independently arrived at similar conclusions to
Charles Darwin concerning the theory of natural selection, often referred to as ‘survival of the fittest’.

to a specific environment, and that leads to the passing on of genetic qualities best suited to that environment,

aware of the controversy they would cause. Wallace wrote to Darwin in 1858 setting out his theory of
natural selection as a mechanism for evolution, which was virtually identical to Darwin's ideas.
Although Darwin suggested that the two present their work together, Wallace graciously declined. He
allowed Darwin to publish his work first, on the grounds that Darwin had spent many years collecting
evidence with which to support it. One viewpoint is that Darwin cheated Wallace of recognition for his
work, but today we acknowledge the efforts of both men. Wallace was also spared much of the religious
backlash Darwin experienced.

Genetic material is found in the form of chromosomes, made of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and
proteins. DNA has a backbone with a tightly-coiled, long double-helix structure (resembling a spiral
staircase). The material of chromosomes is called ‘chromatin’, which means ‘coloured threads’. This is
what genetic material resembles after it has been stained and viewed under a microscope.

| Chromatids: pairs of parallel strands of a duplicated chromosome joined by a single centromere.

When genetic material replicates, the two copies remain attached for a time, While in this state, each
thread-like structure is called a chromatid. The pair are referred to as sister chromatids. This difference
in naming tells us that the genetic material is still undergoing replication, The chromatids are attached
at one area called the centromere. A protein ‘belt’ (a kinetochore) forms around the centromere. Each
part of the sister chromatids is referred to as an arm. The short arms are called p-arms (from the French,
petit meaning ‘small’) and the long arms are q-arms.

\\ Dominant Alleles

When a gene for a characteristic can appear in two different forms, these are called alleles.

The basic unit of inheritance is the gene. When genes are available in alternative forms, these alternative
forms are called alleles. The genes on paired chromosomes control the same characteristic and can give
identical or conflicting instructions to the cells. If the instructions are different, only one gene will be
obeyed. The instructions from one gene will override the other,

The gene that ‘wins’ is called the dominant gene and the one that ‘loses’ is called the recessive gene.
Dominant characteristics will always appear in the first generation offspring (F,). When a dominant trait
(allele) is present, it will always mask the presence of a recessive characteristic (allele). The dominant
allele is represented by an upper-case (capital) letter and the recessive allele by a lower-case letter.
Recessive characteristics only become visible in their ‘pure’ (homozygous) form, when a double dose of
that recessive gene is present, Since we receive one gene from each parent, the only way for the
recessive to be visible in the phenotype (physical characteristic) is if it is the only type of gene passed
‘on by the parents.

}\\ Genetics: an overview

Genetics is a branch of biology. It is the study of inheritance — the passing on of
characteristics from one generation to the next. The term ‘genetics’ was first used by
William Bateson (a British biologist) in 1906.

Although theories of inheritance, or heredity, were put forward at least as early as
the Sth and 4th centuries BC, the study of genetics only truly began in the 18th and
19th centuries. Observations were made of how specific characteristics of plants
and animals were passed on from one generation to the next, to provide a rational
basis for the improvement of crop plants and livestock.

The most significant breakthrough in genetics was made by the Austrian Monk

Gregor Mendel (1822-84). He observed specific features of the pea plant and counted the number of
individuals in which each characteristic appeared through several generations, By concentrating on just
a few features and determining what proportion of each generation received them, he was able to
demonstrate specific patterns of inheritance. These patterns have been shown to be applicable to most
genetic systems,

‘There are two ways in which living things reproduce themselves — sexually and asexually. This sheet
deals with sexual reproduction, which leads to genetic variation,

All animals and plants which reproduce sexually start with a female sex cell (egg or ovum) which is
entered and fertilised by a male sex cell (in animals this is sperm; in flowering plants it is pollen). Sex
cells are called gametes.

The fertilised egg (zygote) grows into a new individual by a series of cell divisions. ‘The new individual
is of the same species and has the characteristics of its parent cells. The ‘recipe’ for this is carried in the
parent gametes. The structures which cause this inheritance of these characteristics are called
chromosomes. Each chromosome is made up of genes — the ‘coded’ instructions for the appearance and
constituents of an organism.

Meiosis _

Meiosis (from the Greek word, meaning ‘to make smaller’) is a more complicated procedure than
mitosis, Both processes involve four phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase. Meiosis
undergoes the process twice and, for this reason, the phases are labelled: prophase I, metaphase I, etc,
and prophase II, metaphase Il, etc. to signify the stage at which the cell is at a given time.

Meiosis divides the nucleus and its contents once, then repeats the procedure a second time. By dividing
the nuclear material twice, the original diploid cell is divided and reassembled as four haploid cells.
Because of this division, and the ‘crossing-over’ of genetic material between chromatids, the four
daughter cells are all genetically different.

In order to help geneticists identify them, chromosomes are numbered in every species. Humans have
46 chromosomes (23 pairs). This is written as 2n = 46, because both parents give us 23 chromosomes,
which totals 46. The numbered chromosomes form homologues.

For example: chromosome 1 will be a certain length and will contain specific genes, perhaps including
one for eye colour. Its homologue, also called chromosome 1, will be the same length and contain the
eye colour gene (but not necessarily coding for the same eye colour). One of the chromosomes will have
been provided by the mother, the other from the father, For each of the 23 chromosomes inherited from
one parent there is (or should be) a homologue. During meiosis, homologous pairs come together,
including a pair of sex chromosomes.

Because humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, the random way in which chromosomes are divided in
meiosis could theoretically give up to 2” different combinations for gametes. The 23rd pair in each set
of human chromosomes is assigned by geneticists to the sex chromosomes, XX for females and XY for
males.

changing DNA (32)

Throughout evolution, random changes have occurred to DNA, These changes can be harmful or
beneficial, depending on how, and in what sort of environment, they are expressed. For example
consider the following scenario. A species of bird has toes. Among this population, through mutation,
some birds carry a gene producing webbed feet. Possession of webbed feet would improve swimming
ability and ability to walk through marshlands. This would enable these birds to be more successful
feeders in wet areas. The webbed-feet birds would breed successfully in wetlands and the trait would

increase through time.
[1] In what ways might the possession of webbed feet be a disadvantage for these birds?

Alternatively, a mutation might debilitate (weaken) an organism. For example, the ability to produce a
vital digestive organism may be reduced or prevented. This would be an example of a harmful mutation.

\\\ Gene Expression: a look at cats

Genetics and environment
The environment in which an organism lives can affect how its genetic information is
expressed. The Siamese cat has a pale coat arising from a mutation in the pigmentation
gene. Pigmentation produces an organism's colour. The Siamese mutation
(selected for by breeders because of the distinct appearance it produces) results
in the chocolate colour only being expressed at the coolest parts of the body. On
cats, these areas are the face, ears, paws and tail.

[1] Give another example of how an organism's environment can affect its phenotype.

[2] Some animats (including humans) have defective pigmentation genes, producing white hair, pale skin and red eyes with a
blue or pink iris, Name this condition,

Random X-inactivation

Another easily recognisable cat is the Calico cat, which has a ‘patchwork’ coat of yellow, black and
white. With the exception of identical twins, no two Calicos will be alike because their colouration is
randomly decided during early development. Fur colour on cats is determined by genes on the X
chromosome and the patchwork results from a process called random X-inactivation. As the name
suggests, certain instructions on the X chromosome are inactivated at random.

Female cats receive two X chromosomes (males receive one). In Calico cats, one chromosome will
contain the black gene (X”) and the other contains the (alternative) yellow gene (X’). As cells divide
during development, one X chromosome in each cell will be inactivated at random. Daughter cells
arising from the original parent cell will possess instructions to grow fur of the remaining colour.
Sometimes the genes are instructed not to produce any colour and this is where the white fur appears.
(Note: linkages to other genes are involved in this.)

\\\\ Genetics Review: terms to know

Reciprocal cross

Whenever we cross a male possessing a specific trait with a female possessing a different trait, the
procedure is called a reciprocal cross. Mendel created reciprocal crosses when he crossed female yellow
peas with male green peas.

[1] What would have been an alternative reciprocal cross using the same characteristics?

1 Filial: to do with a son, daughter, child or offspring.

F, and F, generations

This is a shorthand term for ‘first filial’ and ‘second filial’ generations. The first generation progeny
(offspring) of a reciprocal cross are called the F, generation. The abbreviation F, means, “The resulting
progeny of the reciprocal cross being studied’.

[2] Why do we usually say F, rather than use the complete definition given above?

The F, generation is the progeny of crossing the F, individuals. Members of the F, generation can be
allowed to self-fertilise (in plants) or cross-fertilise with other members of the F, generation. Either way,
the progeny is referred to as the F, generation.

Cell cycle: growth and reproduction
All cells grow and reproduce. They use either of the processes mitosis or meiosis.
Mitosis occurs in somatic cells. These are cells used for growth and development of an organism.

Meiosis is exclusively used by germ cells. Germ cells are involved in reproduction. Male and female
reproductive cells are referred to as gametes. When a female gamete (ovum) is fertilised by a male
gamete (sperm) a zygote is formed.

\\\ Sex and Genes G2A)

Norman human body (somatic) cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes.
In 22 of the pairs, both chromosomes look the same as each other.
In one pair, the chromosomes do not always resemble each other.
In females, these chromosomes are the same, and are called X

chromosomes. In males, one of the chromosomes looks the same as

the X chromosome in the female cells. The other looks different and is called the Y chromosome. So,
human females have 22 pairs of ‘normal’ chromosomes and an XX pair. Human males have 22 pairs of
chromosomes and an XY pair. Extra sex chromosomes are found in about one in 1000 people. The three
most common examples of this are XXY, XYY and XXX.

Genes are grouped together on chromosomes. Those found on X or Y chromosomes are said to be ‘sex-
linked’. The Y chromosome doesn't carry very many genes. It does carry the information to give male
characteristics.

[4] Name two male secondary sexual characteristics

In males, nearly all the genes on the X chromosome, whether or not they are dominant, will affect many
functions, not necessarily related to sex. This means that there is only one form of most genes on the
sex chromosomes of males.

Characteristics controlled by genes.on the X chromosome are sex-linked because they occur more
often in one sex than the other.

Another way of saying this is that the XX chromosomes in a female contain many paired genes. The Y
chromosome in a male does not have partners for most of the genes on the X. So any recessive genes
on the X chromosome will occur more often in males. These unpaired genes on the X chromosome, are
sex-linked.

JA\ Sutton, Boveri and Chromosomes

Chromosomes are clearly seen under a standard light microscope (that is one that uses glass lenses) when
acell is undergoing division. (Note: the cell must be stained first). Chromosomes get their names from two
Greek words, chroma (meaning colour) and somes (meaning body), because they absorb certain dyes.

| Cytology: a branch of biology that deals with the structure and function of celts.

Cytologists had a good idea of the sequences involved in mitosis and meiosis over a hundred years ago.

In the early 1900s biologists began to see that there was a link between the way chromosomes behaved
and (the newly rediscovered) Mendel’s ‘factors’.

Walter Stanborough Sutton was an American physician and geneticist. He (and others) pointed out, in
1902, that Mendel’s hereditary factors (genes) occurred in pairs in somatic cells and separated when
gametes were formed (gametogenesis). This tied in with the fact that somatic cells contain two of each
kind of chromosome and that these chromosomes separate during meiosis. After further study of meiosis
(in grasshoppers) he observed that:

* ina cell undergoing meiosis, the chromosomes line up in pairs

= the chromosomes in each pair resemble each other strongly in physical appearance

* at one stage the chromosome pairs separate, giving each resultant gamete (sex cell) only one
chromosome from the pair

* when a male sex cell and a female sex cell unite, the resulting zygote has a full complement of
chromosomes.

Around the same time, Theodor Heinrich Boveri, a German zoologist, independently demonstrated the
separate and continuous existence of chromosomes. Boveri is also noted for his discovery of the
centrosome. Between the work of Sutton and Boveri (and other researchers) a chromosome theory of
inheritance started to take shape. The points below summarise Sutton and Boveri's views at the time,

© __ When learning a new scientific concept, it can sometimes be difficult to understand what is going on —

especially when you cannot actually see it. To help you understand, a simple model can be invented to
explain what is happening. However, models do have their limitations and may need to be changed as your
understanding becomes better.

In a circuit the power supply—the battery or the powerpack—acts as an energy bank, supplying the
electrons with the same amount of energy as they travel. As the electrons move around the circuit, they use
some of this energy.

Some materials are more difficult for electrons to move through than other materials. Such materials
cause resistance in a circuit. Materials with low resistance allow the current to pass through easily; they are
good conductors. Materials with high resistance do not allow much current to flow through; they are
resistors. Sometimes the shape and length of the wire affects resistance, for example a thin piece of wire has
a higher resistance than a thicker piece of wire.

Short circuits and fuses — Part 1

12a

}

NWN

In an electric circuit some electrical energy needs to be used up; that is, a resistance must slow the electric
current, otherwise the unusually large amount of current travelling through the circuit will cause some of
the circuit components to heat up, to melt or to spark. When components melt or get wet, electricity will
flow along the path of least resistance, possibly causing a short circuit which often leads to fire. Fuses are
designed to ‘blow’ before any item in a circuit causes a fire. When a fuse blows, the circuit is interrupted
and electricity no longer flows.

Ammeters measure the current. Since they have a very low resistance themselves and do not influence
the current, they are switched in series with the item to be measured. Voltmeters, on the other hand,
measure the potential difference and do not want any current to flow through them. Therefore, a voltmeter
has a very high resistance and is switched parallel with the item to be measured.

Using a seismograph 6a

Anon

Earthquakes are often measured using the Richter scale. The Richter scale is better known than the Mercalli
scale and is used with seismographs. A seismograph is a device that measures the strength of earthquakes.

Building a seismograph

The other day we built and tested a seismograph in our science class. We hung a 2 kilogram weight
from a retort stand, The retort stand had a clamp fixed to its top with a boss head. A strong string
held the weight way below the clamp. The weight was about 5 centimetres above the base of the
retort stand, Then we taped a pen to the weight so that the pen just touched the retort stand base.
Finally we stipped a sheet of paper between the pen and retort stand base. And that was our

seismograph.

Forming a fold
Folds in the lithosphere develop when plastic rock material is pushed together. A section of the lithosphere
is made up of several layers of plastic rock, often sedimentary rock. When great forces push the layers
together, they begin to bend up and down like ocean waves. Because the rock in the layers is plastic and not
brittle, it does not break. As a result, over a long period of time, fold mountains are formed. Examples of fold
mountains include the Alps in central Europe and the Appalachian mountains in east North America.

The rock layers of the earth 2a
Avant

a HEME Read the text below about the layers of the earth.

a_ In the left margin, write the main topic of each paragraph.

The earth is huge ball made of mainly different types of rock. Its total diameter is about
12 500 km and it has four layers: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.

The crust is the outside layer. It is made of solid rock, The thickness of the crust ranges from
5 km under the oceans to 60 km under mountains and is 15 km thick on average. The crust’s
surface temperature is 20°C on average. The crust makes up 2% of the volume of the earth,

The mantle is the second layer and it is 2800 km thick. Its rocky material is molten and like
a thick paste. Its temperature ranges from 800°C near the crust to 2200°C near the outer core.
The mantle makes up 81% of the earth by volume.

The outer core is the third layer. It has completely liquid rock material. The outer core is
2000 km thick. Its temperature is 3600°C near the inner core. The outer core is 16% of the
earth’s volume,

The inner core is the fourth and innermost layer. It contains solid rock material, because the
‘other layers around it compress it with great force. The inner core is 2800 km thick. The
temperature at the centre of the earth is 5000°C and is produced by radioactive decay. The
‘inner core makes up 1% of the earth's volume,

The crust and the solid topmost part of the mantle are also called lithosphere and the liquid
part of the mantle is then called the asthenosphere.

Making a volcano 10

= Volcanoes are the result of weaknesses in the earth's crust. Molten rock (magma) in the magma reservoir
makes its way up through a vent to a crater. The vent is like a pipe that joins the crater to the magma
reservoir. Cone shaped mountains form from the layers of ash and lava. Lava is the term given to the
hardened molten rock that has come out of a volcano. Lava, rocks, ash, water vapour and other gases come
out of the crater. Other features associated with volcanoes, which help volcanologists recognise extinct
volcanoes, are dykes and sills. A dyke is an intrusion of igneous rock (solidified magma) that cuts across
other layers of rock. A sill is an intrusion that cuts parallel through the rock layers,

Explaining acid rain 17a

O00
Acid rain is @ major problem in countries that are industrialised, Such countries tend to release large
amounts of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide into the air. The former gas is emitted into the air by burning
coal, which contains some sulfur, and by extracting metals from sulfide ores. The latter gas comes from the
use of petrol and diesel in cars and trucks.

Nitrogen dioxide gas dissolves in rainwater drops to produce nitric acid. Sulfur dioxide in the
atmosphere also dissolves in water droplets in the air to produce sulfuric acid. As a result of those acids in
the rain drops, acid rain is formed.

Acid rain has a low pH, as low as 3. It is therefore quite acidic. The long-term effects of this rain have
unfortunately lowered the pH of rivers and lakes. This has had a detrimental effect upon fish populations.
Plants also suffer because the soil becomes affected as well. Such effects have been seen in North America
and Scandinavia. In Europe, acid rain has done more damage to statues and old buildings than weathering
has done in the last 400 years.

6 Indicators
Acids and bases change the colour of certain dyes. These dyes are called indicators, Indicators tell us
whether a substance is acidic, basic or neutral. Some indicators in the school laboratory are kept as liquids
in dropper bottles, while others are dried onto strips of paper. Litmus, phenolphthalein, methyl orange and

bromothymol are some common indicators. Indicators can also be made from plants, for example, the
liquid from boiled rhubarb stems turns red in acids and green in bases.

pH scale

The pH paper changes into one of several colours when dipped into a liquid substance, The colour is
matched to numbers on a pH scale, The pH scale gives very acidic solutions the number 1, very basic

atom. This orbital atomic model allows us to explain

Protons and neutrons are 2000 times heavier than electrons. Protons and electrons have an electric charge:

Atomic numbers and mass numbers, atoms and isotopes

Atoms are neutral, although some of their subatomic particles do have an electric charge. But the positive
and negative subatomic charges cancel each other leaving the atom neutral. Therefore, the number of
positive protons must equal the number of negative electrons. The atomic number gives the number of
protons.

Since protons and neutrons are very much heavier than electrons, it is the protons and neutrons which
determine the mass of the atoms. Usually an atom has as many neutrons as protons. The mass number is
the sum of protons and neutrons.

‘Some elements have atoms which have the same number of protons in the nucleus (so the same atomic
number) but more or fewer neutrons (so they have different atomic weights). Their atoms are now called
isotopes.

When the number of neutrons is much larger than the number of protons in a large nucleus, the isotope’s
nucleus is unstable. As a result it breaks up, forming new atoms and giving off radiation.

The periodic table of elements 5a
THY O00

© A brief history
In 1829 scientists knew about 40 elements. German scientist Johann Dobereiner noticed that lithium,
sodium and potassium had very similar properties. Calcium, strontium and barium were also similar to
each other. Chlorine, bromine and iodine formed another triad. In 1864, English scientist John Newlands
replaced the triads with a law of octaves, which was based on the atomic weights of 60 known elements as
well as their properties. Dmitri Mendeleev, from Russia, refined the periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for
some elements which had not been discovered. Mendeleev predicted the properties of some of those
missing elements quite accurately. However, there were some inconsistencies; certain elements were too
heavy for their position in the periodic table. Henry Mosely (England, 1914) resolved these problems, when
he based the order of the elements on their atomic number rather than their weight. Today we know 103
elements and they are all organised into the periodic table of elements.

PartA

The nervous system allows living things to detect what is going on around them. ‘This is called sensitivity.
Any change which the nervous system detects is called a stimulus. The nervous system processes the
information and then a gland or a muscle reacts. This reaction is called a response.

‘The nervous system is made up of the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system. The
central nervous system includes the brain and the spinal cord for many involuntary and automatic
responses. The peripheral nervous system is a network of nerves that spread throughout the body. They
connect the nerve endings in muscles, glands and sense organs to the central nervous system.

Part B
Nerves are made up of special cells called neurones. The bundles of neurones look like the wires in a
telephone cable. These nerve cells carry electric impulses or messages at gfeat speed around the body. There
are three kinds of neurones: sensory neurones carry messages to the central nervous system; motor neurones
carry messages from the brain; and connector neurones carry messages in the brain and spinal cord.

SS

The respiration process ~ an explanation
Photosynthesis catches energy and respiration releases it.

You may have learnt that plants trap energy from the sun and use it to convert low-energy carbon dioxide
and water to high-energy glucose and low-energy oxygen. This process is called photosynthesis, Plants store
their glucose as starch, a complex carbohydrate molecule. Animals obtain their food by consuming plants
or other animals, so they are called consumers. Inside the digestive system of animals, the complex starch
is broken down again into a simpler form, glucose. The glucose travels to the cells and is further broken
down in the process of respiration. During respiration energy is released and made available to the cells. The
cells use the energy for many chemical reactions, as welll as for heat.

‘The sun's energy, which is trapped by the plants during photosynthesis, is released during respiration. In
other words, respiration is an energy-releasing process. It occurs in all living things, in their cells, During
respiration oxygen is used up as the glucose is broken down in many controlled reactions, Carbon dioxide
and water are produced as the waste products. These become the raw materials needed for photosynthesis.

There is a cycle involving photosynthesis and respiration. In this way we do not run out of food, oxygen
and carbon dioxide,

A history of the telescope
Waves
17a
When Phoenicians were cooking on
sand around 3 500 BC, they discovered glass. But
it took thousands of years before glass was shaped
into a lens for the first telescope. Lenses that could
change the magnification of objects were known
in Europe at the end of the thirteenth century. 
The spectacle maker Hans Lippershey
(1570–1619), born in Germany and working in
Holland, is often credited with the invention of
the first telescope in 1608. If one placed a
biconvex lens (a lens used to correct long-
sightedness) about 40 cm away from a biconcave
lens (a lens used to correct short-sightedness) and
then looked through them, distant objects
appeared closer. This spyglass was used for
spotting the army’s enemy.  
The telescope was introduced to astronomy
in 1609 by the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei
(1564–1642), who became the first man to see the
craters of the moon and went on to discover
sunspots, the four large moons of Jupiter and the
rings of Saturn. Galileo’s telescope was a simple
refractor telescope, using a plano-convex lens and
a plano-concave eye lens in a tube. This
arrangement magnified up to 30 times but
provided only a narrow field of view: Galileo
could see no more than a quarter of the moon’s
face. The German Johannes Kepler (1571–1630)
invented the form of the refracting telescope that
is the basis for modern refractors; it has a convex
eye lens. However, Kepler’s telescope produced
large inverted images with some chromatic
distortions (the lenses acted like a prism and split
the starlight into its constituent colours resulting
in coloured fuzzy edges of the images).    
In 1704, Sir Isaac Newton announced a
new concept in telescope design: instead of lenses,
a curved mirror was used to gather in light and
reflect it. This reflecting mirror acted like a light-
collecting bucket. Newton’s reflector telescope

It is possible to predict exactly where the image of an object will appear when that object is in front of a
curved mirror. If you select a point on an object (traditionally the tip of a vertical arrow), draw a couple
of light rays from that point and follow some rules about reflection, you can find the position of the
reflected arrow tip. The position where the two light rays from the object meet or appear to meet after
reflection fixes the image. 
Here are some things about light rays that you need to know to draw concave mirror diagrams:
•
A parallel ray is a ray that is parallel to the axis.
•
A focus ray is a ray that travels through the focus.
•
An incoming ray travels from the object to the mirror.
•
A reflected ray travels away from the mirror.
•
After an incoming parallel ray is reflected, it becomes a reflected focus ray.
•
After an incoming focus ray is reflected, it becomes a reflected parallel ray.
•
If an incoming ray does not hit the mirror, extend it backwards.
•
Reflected rays that don’t seem to meet might do so if they are extended backwards. 
•
If reflected rays do not meet, a clear image is not produced.
•
If the image is on the same side of the mirror as the object, it is a real image. 
•
If the image is on the opposite side of the mirror to the object, it is a virtual image.
Compared to its object, an image can be closer to the mirror, further away or the same distance from the
mirror. It can be smaller, larger or the same size. It can be upright or inverted, and real or virtual.

Reflection, refraction, diffraction, scattering
Waves
10a
Sound and light carry messages from one place to another. Light waves are transverse waves that do not
require a medium for transmission. Sound waves are longitudinal waves that do require a medium for
transmission. Sound and light waves seem to travel in straight lines ... or do they? 
Reflection
Like a bouncing ball, light can bounce off a
surface. The reflected light changes direction
when it bounces off a surface. Measurements
show that the angle of incidence equals the
angle of reflection (the law of reflection).
Smooth surfaces act as mirrors – light rays are
reflected uniformly and form images. Each bit of
a rough surface also obeys the law of reflection,
but the overall effect of the uneven surface is to
scatter the light everywhere. Clear images are
not formed. 
Optical fibres are tubes with an extremely thin
glass core. They are produced so that light will pass along the fibres bouncing off the walls (internal
reflection). As (ideally) no light leaves through the sides, a light ray is able to travel large distances in the
fibre.  
Sound is also reflected. We detect echoes when a reflected sound wave reaches our ears some time after

13a
Our eyes are one of our sense organs. They detect light. 
On the outside, our eyes have protective eyelids. Closed, the eyelids protect eyes from smoke, onions, dust,
bright lights and physical intrusion. The eyelids are surrounded by hairs called eyelashes and by touch
receptors, that work together to protect our eyes. 
Eyes are cleaned and lubricated by tears that are produced in the tear gland. Positioned near the
eyebrows, the glands are not an external feature of the eye. Tears are released through tear ducts found
near the corners of the eyes. 
The coloured part of our eye is called the iris. It is a ring of muscle that changes the size of the pupil, the
dark central area. Light passes through the pupil. If the light is too bright, the iris decreases the size of the
pupil. If there is not much light, the iris increases the size of the pupil. 
A cross-section of the human eye reveals a thin, clear skin, the cornea, that covers the front of the eye. Its
properties allow light to pass through it. All the light that enters the eye is organised by the cornea and
lens. The lens is made from a clear translucent material and is surrounded by a lens muscle. When the
lens muscle relaxes, it becomes a large ring and the lens is made thin; when it contracts, it forms a small
ring and the lens becomes thick. The cornea and lens focus the light rays onto the retina, which is located
at the back of the eyeball. If a viewed object is close to the eye, the lens thickens so that the image of the
object is focused and clear on the retina. For a distant object the eye lens is flattened. The retina has light
receptors that are sensitive to the colours of light and to light brightness. The image of the object is upside
down on the retina. The receptors in the retina send electrical impulses to the brain via the optic nerve,
which is located outside the eyeball

Early telephones contained a carbon microphone in a handheld mouthpiece along with a separate
earpiece, dialing mechanism and other parts. The microphone changed sound waves into varying electric
currents. The earpiece converted varying electric currents from another telephone back into sound waves. 
High pitch sounds have high frequencies and result in electric currents that change direction (alternate)
quickly (with high frequency). Deep or low pitch sounds with their lower frequencies end up as electric
currents with a lower frequency. Soft sounds have vibrations with small amplitudes, while loud sounds
have vibrations with large amplitudes.
A carbon microphone is a small box with two metal plates – one fixed and the other free to vibrate, each
connected by wire with other parts of an electrical circuit. Carbon powder fills the space between the two
plates. When the carbon powder is loosely packed, it conducts electricity poorly. When it is compressed, it
is a better conductor of electricity.
A soft, deep sound hits the free-moving plate (diaphragm) of a carbon microphone resulting in weak and
low frequency vibrations of the plate. These plate vibrations cause weak and low frequency electricity
pulses in the wires leading away from the carbon microphone.

wave has been represented like a transverse wave in the diagram, although it
is really a longitudinal wave. Transverse waves are easier to draw and
differences can be shown clearly, so particular sound waves are often sketched

Isaac Newton – Founder of classical physics
Motion
18a
Isaac Newton was born into a farming family in
Woolsthorpe, England, in 1643. He went to the
Free Grammar School in nearby Grantham. His
school reports described him as idle and
inattentive. Isaac mostly kept his own company
and was known as a sober, silent, thinking lad.
When he did associate with others, it was nearly
always with girls. Isaac is remembered for his
strange inventions and extraordinary inclination
for mechanical works. Among these was a
windmill powered by a treadmill run by a
mouse.
Later, his mother made Isaac leave school in
order to help run the family farm. But with
support from his uncle, Isaac continued his
studies at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1661.
Newton’s aim at Cambridge was a law degree,
but soon he became involved with other topics
like algebra, optics and astronomy. Newton did
a lot of studying of other scientists and ancient
philosophers. 
To test a question about colours, he stared at the
sun with one eye until all the colours changed.
As a result, he had to shut himself up in a dark
room for several days before he could get rid of
the spots floating before his eyes.
Despite some evidence that his progress had not

Mass is defined as the amount of substance in an object. Its base unit is the kilogram (kg).
Weight is a force. It is a force that arises because of gravity. The larger an object, the stronger the gravity
force; so huge objects like stars have strong gravity, which causes things to weigh more there than on
smaller objects. Weight is measured in newtons (N). 
It is common to say ‘My weight is 50 kg’, but this is scientifically incorrect and probably arises from the
confusion between mass and weight that many people have. (A person of mass 50 kg actually has a
weight of 500 N.) We should actually say ‘My mass is 50 kg’.

are taking a giant triple beam balance for measuring our mass and a bathroom scale for our weight. On

Meiosis is a special type of cell division that occurs in the sex organs of animals and plants; for example, in the 
ovaries and testes of animals. Meiosis results in the production of ova, which are eggs (singular: ovum), in females 
and sperm in males. Ova and sperm are also called gametes. Haploid gametes are produced from diploid cells.
Meiosis requires two cell divisions which result in four daughter cells. Each daughter cell has half the number of 
chromosomes as the parent cell (daughter cells are haploid, parent cell is diploid), therefore they are not identical to 
the parent cell nor to each other. Meiosis is often called the reduction division.
