Assignments in Junior Science – Book 7 – Genetics
Cells divide in order to make more cells. Usually the new cells (or daughter cells) are the same as the original ones 
(the parent cells). This type of cell division is called mitosis. Mitosis occurs when organisms grow bigger, when 
organisms replace lost or damaged cells, and when simple organisms reproduce asexually. Sometimes parent cells 
divide to develop into sex cells (or gametes); these egg and sperm contain half the normal number of chromosomes 
and join later during fertilisation to produce the first cell of a new offspring. This type of cell division is called 
meiosis.
When we refer to identical daughter cells, we mean that the chromosomes, which are the carriers of genetic 
information, are exactly the same. The cells themselves are smaller and similar to each other.

Chromosomes with their genes are made up of the chemical DNA or deoxyribonucleic 
acid. DNA is a long molecule that stores all genetic information. It looks like a double 
helix or a twisted ladder, as you can see in the diagram at the right. 
DNA has only four repeated subunits, the nucleotides. In humans, a DNA molecule 
is about 2 cm long. In a 1 mm section of a DNA molecule there can be 8 million 
nucleotides. Each nucleotide is made up of a sugar unit, a phosphate unit and a base unit. 
The phosphate links the sugars to make the long strand (i.e. sugar – phosphate – sugar 
– phosphate – sugar). The bases of one strand lock onto the bases of the other strand to 
form the double strand. 
Although the sugar and phosphate units are all the same, there are four kinds of bases: 
adenosine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T). The bases only join in certain 
pairs: A – T and C – G. In order to code for a particular gene such as tongue rolling, the 
DNA section of a particular chromosome is a certain length and the bases are in a particular order.
1 	Identify the chemicals sugar, phosphate and the four bases of the DNA section by: 
• shading sugar horizontally 
• shading phosphate vertically 
• labelling each base as A, C, G or T.  
One sugar and two bases have been identified for you. 
When a cell divides, it first has to make a copy of its DNA molecules. First, the double helix untwists. Then it splits 
open into two strands. The nucleotides which are floating around in the nucleus come into contact with the open 
strands and matching bases lock together. After a few minutes, two new double strands have been produced. It is 
important that the two new double strands are identical to the original.

Genetic diseases – mutations
Sometimes the codes in genes are changed, and the developing cells receive a wrong message. A change in the codes 
could cause the cells to make a wrong protein, or no protein at all. As a result, the cells do not function normally. 
Changes in the genes are called mutations, derived from a Latin word meaning change. Mutations can be dominant 
or recessive. If dominant, they will be expressed and hide the normal form of the gene. If recessive, the normal gene 
will hide the mutation. To have the characteristic of the recessive mutation, a person must have both genes with that 
mutation.

The Tasmanian tiger, thylacine, is a marsupial carnivore that used 
to live in Tasmania. European settlers believed this animal to be 
dangerous to them and their farm animals and so started hunting it 
down. The last thylacine died in captivity in 1936. Some scientists 
want to clone a thylacine and reintroduce it to Tasmania, but there are 
arguments against as well as in favour of this issue.
Thylacines were native animals of Tasmania. It was only because 
European settlers feared them that they were exterminated. Had 
the European people not murdered this indigenous marsupial, the 
thylacine would still be living in Tasmania today. Reintroducing cloned 
Tasmanian tigers would only make right the wrong done by people of 
the past. 
Cloning technology for animals exists. Scientists know how to clone 
animals and have cloned many already: sheep, cows, goats, cats and 
mice are some examples. Although an extinct animal has not been 
cloned, with some more research scientists could do that too. There is 
no scientific technology standing in the way of cloning the Tasmanian 
tiger.

What does genetics have do with me?
Has anyone ever told you that you have your father’s nose or your grandmother’s hair? Many of our features are 
inherited from our parents, and theirs from their parents. Inheritance or heredity is the passing of characteristics

We all inherit slightly different combinations of these features from our parents. Even brothers and sisters look 
different, because they inherit different characteristics from their parents.

Genetics
All organisms are made of cells, and each type of organism has a particular number of chromosomes. For example, 
each body cell of a dog has 28 chromosomes, while each body cell of a horse has 64 chromosomes. Human cells 
contain 46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs of chromosomes, or 2 sets of 23 chromosomes (= 2n).
Reproductive cells – sperm in males and eggs (ova) in females – always contain half the number of chromosomes of 
the body cells; that is, one set of 23 chromosomes (= 1n). This ensures that the baby also has 46 chromosomes, not 
92. When an egg and sperm join during fertilisation, 23 chromosomes come from the mother and 23 come from 
the father. The fertilised egg has a complete set of 46 chromosomes; that is, 23 pairs of chromosomes. 
1 	What do you think would happen if the egg and sperm always had a complete set of chromosomes?
2 	Find the terms ‘diploid’ and ‘haploid’ in figure 1. What do you think these terms mean?
A special pair of chromosomes determines whether the fertilised egg will be a boy or a girl. This pair is made up 
of the sex chromosomes. In males, one chromosome in this pair is smaller. The larger chromosome is called X and 
the smaller is called Y. Females have two X chromosomes, which are the same size. Males have X and Y. These X 
and Y chromosomes are called sex chromosomes, because they contain the genes that determine sex. The other 
chromosomes are called autosomes, and these include all the other pairs of chromosomes. Each pair of autosomes 
in the human karyotype is numbered.
Figure 2 shows the karyotype of a human female and a human male. The first 22 pairs of chromosomes are the 
autosomes. The 23rd pairs are the sex chromosomes.

Read the text about cloning and then complete the task on the next page.
Explanation of cloning
A clone is an organism which is genetically identical to another organism. Cloning is a form of asexual reproduct-
ion which is widespread in nature. For unicellular organisms and many plants, it is a normal process, such as cell 
division or vegetative propagation. Mammals can produce identical twins when very young embryos split in two. 
However, artificial cloning is the cause of much debate. There are two types of artificial cloning: embryo splitting 
and nuclear transfer. 
• Embryo splitting is similar to the production of twins or multiple births, except it does not happen naturally – 
it is brought about by a scientist or doctor. In this type of cloning, the clones are the same age. 
• During nuclear transfer, the complete set of chromosomes of one individual (the genetic parent) is transferred 
into a stem cell of another individual (the cell donor parent) and carried by a third individual (the host parent). 
This method allows the chromosomes to be transferred at different times and so the clones can be of completely 
different ages. For example, a pet cat that has died could be cloned for its owners. 
It is also possible to transfer only part of a chromosome of an individual to a complete set of chromosomes of 
another individual. For example, a strawberry could carry a fish gene to prevent it from freezing at very low 
temperatures. This method produces transgenic species, which could not be produced in nature. 
While embryo splitting has a fairly high success rate, nuclear transfer has often resulted in the death of the new 
clones or in new clones with health or development problems. Dolly, the cloned sheep, was one survivor of 300 
clones. The diagram below outlines the process involved in producing Dolly the cloned sheep.

Genetics
The first studies of inheritance were carried out by Gregor Mendel in 1866. He studied many characteristics of the 
garden pea and eventually discovered that inheritance followed precise rules. Mendel chose peas because normally 
pea plants are self-fertilising and their pollination can be controlled. His research involved careful planning. He 
used thousands of plants and experimented over eight years. Mendel became the first scientist to understand the 
importance of statistics in investigations and to apply mathematics to biological problems.
Mendel’s first step was to spend two years growing the same peas, ensuring each flower fertilised itself. During 
fertilisation, pollen from stamens containing the male sperm fuse with a female egg in order to produce a seed.
Every time Mendel’s offspring plants looked the same as the parent plants. In this way Mendel made sure that the 
plants were purebred – that is, their chromosomes were homozygous.

Up, up and away – a hot air story
The story of the invention of the hot air balloon begins in the small town of Alchemy in southern 
France. Two brothers, Joseph and Jacques Montgolfier, were in the paper manufacturing business. 
They noticed that whenever they burnt paper, the ashes floated up into air. They discovered that the 
smoke and heat from the burning paper had a lifting quality.
With this in mind, the brothers set out to design a craft that could capture the heat and smoke 
to allow the craft to lift off the ground. On 19th September 1783, the Montgolfier brothers were 
successful in creating and launching their invention: a hot air balloon.
Their hot air balloon was made from paper and cloth. They used a combination of chopped wool, 
straw and dried horse manure for burning in order to inflate the balloon. The straw provided the 
heat which heated the air inside the balloon. The wool and manure made lots of smoke and kept the 
flame low so the paper and cloth balloon did not catch fire.
The brothers were a little unsure how the balloon would fly or how safe it was, so they sent sheep, 
chicken and ducks up in their balloon. Their trials were a success – they managed to keep the 
animals floating for eight minutes and then land the balloon successfully.
On 21st November 1783, the Montgolfier brothers convinced the King of France to come and see 
their invention. This time, people would be on board instead of farm animals. Two of their best 
friends volunteered for the job. The balloon was successfully launched and rose about 150 m above 
the rooftops of Paris and successfully landed in a vineyard a few kilometres away.

Of course you know that the fridge is cold on the inside. But did you also know that a fridge is warm at the back on 
the outside?  How does the fridge get so cold inside? And why is it warm behind the fridge?
In most fridges, there is a system of pipes on the inside and the outside. The inside pipes are usually fused onto a 
silver coloured metal plate. Outside at the back, the pipes are connected to many small black metal plates. Where 
the pipes enter the interior, there is an expansion valve. There is also an electric motor, which is usually under the 
fridge at the back. This motor runs a compressor.
Inside the pipes is a refrigerant. In old fridges this is Freon, which boils at -30°C. But Freon is one of the gases that 
destroy the ozone layer in the atmosphere and so it is no longer used. Old fridges should have their Freon taken out 
professionally. Freon destroys ozone molecules in the atmosphere and so they cannot absorb the dangerous and 
skin-cancer causing ultraviolet rays from the Sun. These days, different refrigerants are used; for example, ammonia 
which boils at -32°C and HFC which has a boiling point of -27°C.

Assignments in Junior Science – Book 8 – Energy and matter
The term thermodynamics comes from the Greek language; thermo has to do with heat, a form of energy, and 
dynamics refers to movement. So thermodynamics is about how heat energy moves. Three important laws of 
thermodynamics were developed in the mid 19th century and the early 20th century. 
8a
The three laws of thermodynamics
The first law of thermodynamics: Conservation of energy
Energy changes from one form to another, it cannot be created or destroyed. Energy is always 
conserved. The total amount of energy in the universe stays constant.
When a bar heater gives off heat and also some light, these forms of energy have come from another 
energy form: electric energy. Neither the heat nor the light were created.
Einstein’s famous equation E = mc 2 broadened this law. The total amount of energy and matter in 
the universe stays the same. Therefore, people are able to change some matter into huge amounts of 
energy, like in a nuclear reactor. In this case, the energy did not come from another form of energy, it 
came from matter. The law of conservation of energy is only true when the amount of matter stays the 
same, which is most of the time.
The second law of thermodynamics: Entropy
The word entropy means messiness or disorder. Energy systems increase their entropy; that is, they 
become more and more messy. Look at your bedroom – after a few days, it can look really untidy. Its 
entropy has increased. If everything in your room ends up on the floor, the potential energy (here 
gravitational potential energy) has become less. Over time there is more entropy – that is, more 
chaos, more disorder, more mess – less orderliness and less potential energy.
Furthermore, heat travels from hotter objects to colder ones in order to make everything equally 
warm. Then it is no longer an ordered system, where heat would be ‘over here’ and cold

Improving cell theory
Scientists improve their theories as new evidence is collected. The idea of cells changed 
over a long time as more evidence was found.
 
l  1665 – Robert Hooke first saw and named cells. Possibly the first theory would have 
begun as: There are some cells in living things.
 
l  1839 – Matthias Schlieden and Theodor Schwann revised the original idea to read: 
All living things are made from cells.
 
l  Soon after, Schlieden and Schwann decided that the theory should be revised to 
include a reference to the materials that cells make, such as bone matrix.
 
l  1858 – Rudolf Virchow added the idea that all cells come from other cells. He is now 
believed to have copied this idea from Robert Remak. 
The theory was then very close to the definition we use today: 
All living things are made from cells and their products. All cells come from other cells.
Science is open to change, but the changes will only be accepted if they are very strongly 
supported and not able to be disproved.

Single lens to compound microscope
The first microscope was used in the 1500s. Over time, 
microscope technology has steadily improved. As the 
technology improved so did knowledge about microbes – 
living things that are too small to see with the naked eye.
 
l  At first, specimens were magnified with single 
lenses. Some of the scientists involved at the time 
were Sacharias Jansen in around 1595, Robert Hooke 
in 1665 and Antonj van Leeuwenhoek in 1653.
 
l  Hooke and Jansen later used two lenses in a row, 
sometimes inside a barrel. These were the first 
compound microscopes.
 
l  Hooke was the first to try shining a light directly onto the specimen.
 
l  Van Leeuwenhoek was first to see pond life protozoa, spirogyra and sperm of 
many animals.
 
l  Hooke made very thin slices of cork that let light through, and saw little 
compartments, which he named cells.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
20
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
New imaging technology
Medical technology has improved greatly over time, 
and doctors now have many ways of looking inside 
patients without cutting them open. 
X-rays don’t pass through bone, so they can make 
an image of the bone like a shadow on a film or screen. 
X-rays can pass through soft tissue in varying amounts, 
making shadows that are weaker than bone images. 
A CAT scan is a computer controlled series of X-rays 
that shows an area of the body in a series of ‘slices’. This 
allows doctors to see tumours or injuries.
Ultrasound vibrations are used to make an image of an internal organ such as a heart,  
or of an unborn baby. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) uses large magnets and radio 
waves to make a three-dimensional image.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
46
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Cholera
In 1854 London was suffering from an outbreak of cholera, a deadly disease. Nobody 
knew how the disease was spread. At that time, people had to get their water from pumps 
in the street. John Snow wondered if cholera was being spread by contaminated water. 
He made a map showing where the cases of cholera were occurring, and discovered that 
most cases were around Broad Street. John Snow broke the handle off the Broad Street 
pump so nobody could pump drinking water from it. 
London’s drinking water came from pools in underground beds of gravel or from 
underground streams. Sewage had leaked into the water, spreading cholera. John Snow 
is now known as the Father of Epidemiology (the study of the spread of disease). He 
saved dozens of lives.
+ 1 How can natural disasters (for example, floods, cyclones, earthquakes, tsunamis) 
lead to cholera outbreaks? 
 
 
2 Military Response teams and organisations such as the Red Cross often rush to disaster 
zones with supplies of clean drinking water. Why? 
 
In modern times when a nation reports an epidemic, large scale international teamwork 
between doctors and governments takes place to control the disease. Disease outbreaks 
such as SARS are controlled by international cooperation.
+ 3 Write down four things you think governments might do to control an 
international disease outbreak.

A great Australian scientist
Imagine you are walking along a corridor. It is 1965. You can

at the bench with an egg in his hand.
You have stumbled upon Sir Frank Macfarlane Burnet 
(1899–1985) who won a Nobel Prize for his work in 
immunology, the study of disease resistance, in 1960. 
Mac, as his colleagues knew him, was Australia’s most celebrated scientist. He 
researched dozens of topics in immunology and virology (the study of viruses) as well 
as other areas, including ageing.
Burnet used egg membranes to grow viruses, including the influenza virus, which is 
related to bird viruses. While he was a great thinker, he was also a practical scientist who 
spent half of each day in his laboratory conducting experiments.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
34
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Fred Hollows
Although he was originally a New Zealander, Fred Hollows is one of Australia’s most 
famous scientists – he was even named Australian of the Year in 1990.
In the 1960s Hollows helped to set up the first Aboriginal Medical Service. By 2005, 
there were more than 60 of them around Australia. As an eye specialist he was horrified 
to learn that many Indigenous Australians were blind from trachoma – a preventable and 
treatable eye disease. Hollows did many trachoma repair operations himself and started 
up the National Trachoma and Eye Health Program to inform Australians, to raise funds 
and to carry out operations.
Hollows didn’t stop there. He and his teams visited many poor countries to carry out 
operations; they even set up a lens factory in desperately poor Eritrea. When he became 
terminally sick with cancer he set up the Fred Hollows Foundation, an organisation that 
works to prevent avoidable blindness and to improve Indigenous Australians’ health. Since 
1992 the Foundation has worked in more than 30 countries in Asia, Africa, Australia and 
the Pacific. The one millionth intraocular lens (a device used to treat cataracts, which cause 
blindness) was inserted in 2003.
Fred Hollows helped millions of people, and his legacy continues to help millions more.

with him to treat trachoma and other eye [diseases/glasses]. He [raised/wasted] money 
from people, governments and companies to [support/delay] his efforts. Many [nasty/
harmless] eye diseases happen in places where people are very [poor/wealthy]. Hollows 
and his teams went to these places to help hundreds of thousands of people. He was a 
great Australian and a great [New Zealander/Canadian].

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
32
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Immunisation and the media
We rely on the media to provide us with information. However, we need to be aware 
of how the information is being presented, and whether all the information is being 
reported. How often have you seen a news story saying that everything is all right? Good 
news stories are not very dramatic, so we don’t see them in the news very often. 
The topic of immunisation is one that people have different opinions about. 
Immunisation can save millions of lives by preventing the spread of disease. However, 
there have also been stories of immunisation having terrible consequences, such as brain 
damage, in children. These stories may sometimes be reported more widely than the 
success stories.
It is important to study the news and history while also asking questions such as:
 
l What is the risk of the vaccine?
 
l What is the risk of the disease it is trying to stop?
 
l Is the risk just to my child or others as well?
Reading the news in this way allows individuals to form a considered opinion. 
+ 1 A local headline read ‘Children ill after National Vaccination Program’. As a result, 
worried parents asked questions at the local medical clinic. Match the answers 
given to each question below.

ACHIEVE!   Science as a human endeavour – Biology for years 7–8
31
© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Nanotechnology
A nanoparticle is tiny. It is a molecule or part molecule and is sometimes called a 
nanomolecule. They can travel easily through blood vessels and enter some cells. 
Scientists are trying to find ways to use these tiny chemical particles in medicine.  
Possible uses could be:
 
l  coating a medicine with nanoparticles so it goes only to the organ where it 
is needed
 
l  attaching nanoparticles to a medicine so it can cross through a body barrier,  
such as from blood into the brain
 
l  to give small doses of medicine that isn’t wasted in other body parts because  
it only goes where it is needed
 
l protecting a vaccine so it can get into the cells where it can work
 
l delivering dangerous chemotherapy drugs directly to the cancer cells only
 
l finding damaged cells and repairing them
 
l attaching nanoparticles to a tumour to make it visible to imaging machines
 
l making purer medicines to reduce side effects caused by impurities.
Nanotechnology requires many years more research. Because the nanoparticles are 
so small and not enough is known about them yet, there are possible dangers. Will they 
stay in the body long after their use is over? Will they stay unchanged in the body or could 
they change and cause problems? Will they get into the environment and cause pollution 
problems? These possible dangers are studied in nanotoxicology.

© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Cleaning up Australia

Wetland rescue
Until the 1980s, Feral Water Buffalo were allowed to graze in the Northern Territory’s 
Kakadu National Park. They damaged native wildlife and their hard hooves compressed 
the ground in many places. After the Feral Water Buffalo had been removed from the 
area, a native grass called Mudja grew wildly and choked off wetlands. Local people had 
previously burned the Mudja grass so other plants could grow. Senior traditional owner 
Violet Lawson taught CSIRO Indigenous research officers Sandra McGregor – her  
daughter – and Peter Christophersen the burning method.

Feral plants and animals
When plant and animal species from other places are introduced into Australia they can 
threaten our unique wildlife, which has little defence against introduced species. Feral 
imported species such as rabbits and foxes can cause huge damage.
Australia is isolated – only Indonesia and Papua New Guinea are nearby. This means 
that few non-native animals and plants have found their way to Australia by themselves. 
However, some have been brought in by humans, either intentionally or accidentally. 
The Australian quarantine service [AQIS] works to prevent any new species from being 
introduced into Australia and harming the environment.

© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Breeding humans?
The biggest danger with organ and tissue transplants is rejection. A patient’s body 
will see a new organ as an invader and try to get rid of it. Transplant recipients 
must take anti-rejection drugs to stop this from happening. The drugs are called 
immunosuppressants, because their job is to suppress the immune system. 
Rejection is less likely to occur if the organ comes from a close relative. Identical  
twins are the best match, and a brother or sister may be the next best.
Imagine you could grow a copy of yourself – then you would have the perfect match if 
you ever needed a transplant! But would that be fair on the other ‘you’, who only existed to 
donate organs? Acts like that could be illegal. 
Apart from laws, doctors also have rules about treatment called medical ethics. 
Government health departments and hospitals have ethics committees. The committees 
make rules that say which medical actions are right and wrong.

another person.

l A heavy smoker receives a lung transplant from a dead  
accident victim. 
 
 
l Have a second child so they can donate a kidney to an  
existing child. 
 
 
l Purchase a kidney from a poor person in a developing country. 
 
 
l Buy a transplant heart from a secret supplier in another country.

Spray-on skin
Spray-on skin is an invention used to help patients 
regrow new skin after suffering severe burns. It was 
developed in Australia by Professor Fiona Wood, 
a plastic surgeon, and Marie Stoner, a scientist. To 
make spray-on skin, skin cells are taken from the 
patient. They are mixed with liquid food and grown 
for five days, then sprayed onto the burn using a 
special cell sprayer. New skin grows very quickly. 
Spray-on skin was used to treat victims of the 2002 
Bali bombings.

© Keith McTaggart and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Developments in selective breeding
Success with wheat breeding
William Farrer was one of the first people to improve wheat crops so they could grow in 
Australian conditions. Farrer developed the basis for a good wheat crop, which has heads 
level for harvesting, high grain yield, makes excellent flour and resists disease – especially 
a mould called rust.
Problem with wheat breeding
The sets of genes that plants in a crop have are almost identical. This makes them 
susceptible to disease. The wild originals of the plant may have genes for disease 
resistance that are no longer present in the crop plants. 
During the mid-1900s, Russian scientist Nikolai Vavilov and others, 
such as CSIRO’s Sir Otto Frankel, suggested that wild seeds of crops 
be placed in freezer storage in case we ever need to reverse the 
specialisation of crops by back-breeding.

Selective breeding
Selective breeding means that a human controls which plants reproduce or which 
animals have offspring. The human chooses parent plants or animals with desirable 
features and avoids those with unwanted features. New techniques in selective breeding 
have been introduced over the last 60 years.

Greenhouse gas from farm animals
Animals that chew cud, such as cattle and sheep, are called ruminants. A part of their 
intestines called the rumen, which is one of four stomachs, contains billions of bacteria 
and protozoa that help to break up grass into useful nutrients. This produces methane 
gas, which is a greenhouse gas, as a by-product. Greenhouse gas from farm animals 
accounts for about 10 per cent of Australia’s greenhouse gas emissions. CSIRO scientists 
are trying to find ways to reduce emissions of methane gas from cattle and sheep. They 
have three projects underway:
 
l study of gut microbes in ruminants
 
l measuring methane emissions from cattle
 
l  investigating how anti-microbial properties contained in different foods affect the 
microbes in the rumen.

foregut] that break down grasses differently and produce far less methane than

Climate change in the news

Rocky Cove’s sea wall will increase in height from 1 metre to 12 metres. Council

Rocky Cove residents who do not believe in climate change held a rally at the sea wall.

Funafuti Airport (destination code FUN) said that the low-lying coral islands may become 
permanently flooded if water levels rise by a metre over the next 100 years. Global 
warming may just be a distant concern to the rest of the world, but in Tuvalu it is looming  
as a disaster.

Different types of water
In many parts of Australia, water is often in short supply. There are different types, or 
grades, of water, and not all of them are safe to drink. Drinking water can be used for 
anything but should not be wasted. Storm water is the water that runs off after a heavy 
rainfall. It is safe to drink if carefully stored. Grey water is not safe for drinking and cannot 
be stored for long, but can be used to water gardens. Black water is dangerous and 
smelly until after it has been treated.

Irrigation – Benefits and challenges
Australia is a dry continent. However, some parts of Australia, such as far north 
Queensland, sometimes receive very high rainfall. When this happens, the water flowing 
along rivers is collected in reservoirs and directed to dry areas. This water is used for 
crops in a process called irrigation. Irrigation means that instead of only growing grass 
and tough shrubs, farmers have enough water to grow citrus and other fruit trees,  
grass for dairy cattle, grapes, rice and vegetables. Although irrigation helps farmers  
to grow crops, it also creates some problems.

in their work. Engineering is one example of a field that uses science. There are many

works with other specialists. A civil engineer would also work with architects, electrical 
engineers, and others.

Working together in Antarctica
Antarctica is a frozen continent that surrounds the South Pole. It is too cold for anyone to 
live there permanently, but it is a unique environment that fascinates many people. It has 
been a place of international cooperation for more than 60 years, with people from all 
over the world working together and sharing their resources and research.
+ 1 The following fictional story parts are out of order. Number the order they should 
appear in for the story to make sense. 
   Four scientists were collecting ice samples on an expedition to find out more 
about climate change.
   The Italians arranged for an aircraft to be put on standby at USA’s McMurdo 
base.
   The scientists were Linda, an Australian, Georges, a Frenchman, Luigi, an 
Italian, and Julio, an American.
  He had a broken leg and his hand was crushed.
  So, Linda contacted the Italian base by radio.
  The scientists managed to hoist Luigi to the surface.
  One day Dr Luigi Volta crashed into a crevasse on his snow mobile.
  But foggy weather made that unavailable.
  From there he was flown to Hobart, where microsurgeons repaired his hand.
   They were working 80 km inland from Italy’s Marco Zucchelli scientific base 
in Terra Nova Bay.
   His leg was set and he went from Casey to France’s Dumont D’Urville base by 
small aircraft for more treatment.
   Instead, a helicopter picked up Luigi and flew him to Australia’s Casey base 
for treatment.
2 Describe in your own words how scientists can help each other in Antarctica.

UNESCO
UNESCO stands for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. 
It was set up by 37 member nations in November 1945. UNESCO’s mission is to promote 
peace and sustainable development and to reduce poverty through education, the 
sciences, culture, communication and information.

Do you believe in science?
It is difficult to believe in science because the whole point of science is not to believe. 
Every fact or law of science is based on what we call a hypothesis. A hypothesis is a 
theory. It can be accepted as true for two reasons:
 
l there is a large amount of supporting evidence
 
l it has not been disproven.
When both of these reasons apply, it has been accepted as science. People sometimes 
use the second point alone to manipulate information. For example:
 Aliens built the pyramids. This has been scientifically proven because it has not 
been disproven.
What evidence is there? A spacecraft landing zone beside the Sphinx? Be wary of  
the words ‘scientifically proven’. Science has strongly supported hypotheses, not proof. 
New evidence may arrive any day to improve or disprove a hypothesis. Most famous 
scientists have had their brilliant hypotheses changed at some point.
+ 1 Underline the statements that you think could be called unsupported hypotheses.

l A parachutist falls slowly enough to reach the ground safely.
 
l My grandma tells fortunes. She said I’d meet a handsome, dark-haired boy  
and I did.
 
l The forecast says it will rain tomorrow.

Who works scientifically?
It is not only scientists who think and work scientifically. The character traits and behaviour 
of scientists are qualities and skills that are needed in all different kinds of work.
Activity sheet – Addressing  
environmental concerns
+ 1 Look at the list of careers below. List the numbers of the qualities listed above 
that you think would help in each career. 
2  Tick any careers that have more than three qualities listed.
 Motor mechanic  
  Fast food restaurant manager  
 
 Librarian  
 Factory safety officer  
 Police officer  
 Accountant  
 Child care worker  
 Teacher  
 Building site worker  
 Nurse  
3 Which of the careers received a tick? 
 
 
 
 
Scientists need to:
1. be curious
2. be observant
3. keep records
4. rely on evidence rather than hearsay 
or old beliefs
5. measure accurately
6. check hypotheses by testing
7. think of explanations and test them
8. improve explanations when new 
evidence is discovered
 9. collect and share evidence
10. encourage others to check for 
accuracy
11. communicate
12. have passion for their work
13. be patient and accurate
14. be creative in seeking answers
15. care about the effects of their work
